tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

A quotient that is not whole stays `n / d` in lowest terms and defaults to a `QQ`. 134	
135	**The change.** The team's compiled path typed a numeral by its prelude's `IntLiteral` or `FloatLiteral` and converted it when the program ran: its code generator emitted an `FIntLiteral` value and a call of the prelude's `coerce_ZZ32` on it at each evaluation, the pair its bytecode optimizer's `RemoveLiteralCoercions` pass matched (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/compiler/asmbytecodeoptimizer/RemoveLiteralCoercions.java:33-51` at b5b0f82c13; `compiler/runtimeValues/FIntLiteral.java` at b5b0f82c13). Now no numeral value exists at run time on the compiled path: each place of a numeral holds one value made before the program runs, a JVM constant where the compile-time evaluation of the place's type's own coercion from the numeral's type ends in an `int`, `long`, `float` or `double` (`ZZ32`, `ZZ64`, `NN32`, `NN64`, `RR32`, `RR64`), and otherwise a static final filled once when the component's class loads, by one call of that coercion compiled as a method of the numeral's four numbers as `ZZ` values (`ZZ`, a program's own types); a place whose type names a type parameter of its generic declaration still calls that method at each evaluation (row 957), and a coercion whose body spawns a task fails the class's load (row 971). A program's type's prefix minus on a negative constant runs once in that static final. Under walk, a folded constant at a library number type converts from its exact value. Tests: `ProjectFortress/library_tests/NumeralFoldIntegers.test`, `NumeralFoldFloats.test`, `ProjectFortress/compiler_tests/NumeralAcrossComponent.test`, `NumeralMinusOnceCompiled.test`, `NumeralCoercionOnceCompiled.test`, `ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/compiler/desugarer/NumeralCoercionFoldJUTest.java`, `ProjectFortress/tests/NumeralFoldedConstantLibraryWalk.fss`. The reason: the Working Draft gives numerals types of their own so that "library designers [can] decide how numerals should interact with other types of objects by defining coercion operations", and has the libraries define the coercions into the number types (`Specification-1.0-frozen/basic/expressions/literals.tex:132-148`); a numeral's coercion called at run time per numeral failed for a coercion of another component, "java.lang.NoClassDefFoundError: NumeralAcrossComponentApi$v".
136	
137	**Provenance.** P-174 and P-176, and the snapshot's section 11 on the library's own types (`explorations/coordinator/postmortem-2026-11-09-numerals/design-snapshot.md`); forks A1 (the fold over a closed fragment), A2 (one method per numeral coercion), A3 (folded constants from their exact value) and A8 (the deleted classes) of climb batch 29b's record; the static numerals probe's patch; rung A of climb batch 29b.
138	
139	### T (`rung-static-numerals-spec`, `fcfd0aeb31`)
140	
141	**The change.**
142	- The team's source: the Working Draft gives a numeral six types, `NaturalNumeral[\n,10,v\]` (and `Literal[\v\]` without leading zeros), `NaturalNumeralWithExplicitRadix[\n,r,v\]`, `RadixPointNumeral[\n,m,10,v\]`, `RadixPointNumeralWithExplicitRadix[\n,m,r,v\]` and `Numeral[\n,m,r,v\]` above all (`Specification-1.0-frozen/basic/expressions/literals.tex:83-129`), says that "Numerals are not directly converted to any of the number types" (`:132-141`) and that libraries define coercions from numerals (`:146-148`), and says nothing of a numeral's value when a program runs or of when a coercion is applied. The team's compiled library types numerals by run-time values, `trait IntLiteral` and `trait FloatLiteral` with getters such as `asZZ32` and `asRR64` (`ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/CompilerBuiltin.fsi:390`, `:479`, at b5b0f82c13), whose coercions run on that value.
143	- What the text now says: a numeral's type exists only at compile time, `NaturalNumeral[\n, r, v\]` or `RadixPointNumeral[\n, m, r, v\]`, at the Draft's arities with the radix as `r`, below a `Numeral` without static parameters; the explicit-radix types and `Literal` are not built; no value of a numeral type exists when a program runs, so a numeral type has no method, no `asFloat` and no `=` with a number type; every number type, the library's and a program's, takes a numeral through `coerce[\nat n, nat r, nat v\](x: NaturalNumeral[\n, r, v\])` or its radix-point form, whose body reads the four numbers as `ZZ` values; the compiler folds it to a constant, or makes the value once per place; `-3` at a program's type is the type's own `-` on the coercion's result for `3`; a `where` clause over the four numbers refuses a numeral statically (`Specification/basic/expressions/literals.tex:98-285`; `Specification/appendices/changes.tex:5010-5486`). The tests that show the tree doing so land with the code: `ProjectFortress/tests/NumeralStaticDesignWalk.fss`, `ProjectFortress/tests/NumeralOwnTypeWalk.fss`, `ProjectFortress/tests/NumeralTypeNoValueWalk.fss`, `ProjectFortress/compiler_tests/NumeralStaticDesignCompiled.fss` and `ProjectFortress/compiler_tests/XXXNumeralWhereRefusedCompiled.test`.
144	- The reason, as evidence: the Draft's own ground, "This approach allows library designers to decide how numerals should interact with other types of objects by defining coercion operations" (`Specification-1.0-frozen/basic/expressions/literals.tex:142-145`), which a coercion that sees only a value cannot carry out: a 16-bit float type's coercion from the four numbers rounds `1.00390625000000000001` once, to `0x3F81`, where a coercion from an `RR64` gives `0x3F80` (`ProjectFortress/compiler_tests/NumeralStaticDesignCompiled.fss`, "BF16(1.00390625000000000001) rounds once, to 0x3F81"); a JVM class file holds no object constant, so a value at a place is a constant or a field filled once when the class loads; the team's own word on the run-time value, "IntLiterals should always be transient objects with minimal lifetime" (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/compiler/runtimeValues/FIntLiteral.java:21-23` at b5b0f82c13).
145	
146	**Provenance.** The curator's design of the static numerals, confirmed on 9 November 2026 (P-174, P-176), with P-173's conversion, default and fold, P-40's bound for sizes, P-165's `asFloat` and P-37's exception for the prelude; the specification written in the revision form (P-96) by climb batch 29b's rung T, with the forks T1 (the entry rewritten in place), T2 (the binary chapter) and T3 (the constant chapter) at their defaults, and the Effects from the forks A1 to A8 of the same batch.

120	- Tasks can write different elements of one array in parallel (`Specification/basic/memory-model.tex`, "Programming Discipline").
121	
122	So `acc := acc + x` inside a parallel `for`, with no `atomic`, is a race. The suites run at four threads, once each, so a race can show in them. A passing run does not prove that there is none.
123	
124	Inside an `atomic` block, the compiled code tracks each mutable variable that the block reads or writes. From the switch-over, it also tracks each array element that the block reads or writes (`references/compiler.md`).
125	
126	## Fortress as a language
127	
128	Each point below corrects an assumption from a language that you know. `references/tests-writing.md` gives the form of a program.
129	
130	- **Dispatch is on every argument, at run time.** A call chooses among overloads by the run-time types of all its arguments, as in Julia, not by static types as in Java. The checker accepts two overloads only if their parameter types exclude each other, one is strictly more specific, or a third covers their meet. The more specific one's return type must fit the other's. Walk checks part of this at load.
131	- **Functional methods.** A method with `self` among its parameters is called `f(x)`, not `x.f()`. It overloads with top-level functions. Most operators are declared so: `opr +(self, other: T): T`. A functional method's name is reserved in every program that imports it, so do not name a variable after it. One type must not have a dotted and a functional method of the same name.
132	- **Traits and objects, no classes.** A trait has methods and abstract fields, and extends several traits. An object is a leaf. `excludes {A, B}` says that no value has both types. `comprises {A, B}` says that every value has a listed type, near Scala's `sealed`. No type may extend two instantiations of one generic trait. This exclusion rule is why the number types are flat (below).
133	- **Static parameters.** They are written `[\T\]`, and `[i]` indexes. Their kinds are types, sizes (a `nat` or `int` parameter used as a value is a `ZZ32`: `references/revival-changes.md`, "Numbers"), `bool` and `opr`. Generics are invariant: there is no `+T` or `-T`. An unbounded type parameter is bounded by `Any`, which holds tuples, functions and `()`, as `Object` does not. A type parameter that a call does not fix takes its bound. Under walk, one whose bound names the parameter itself stays open, and every value passes it. Walk instantiates a reduction or a comprehension without static arguments at the type declared for its value: a local variable's type, or a top-level or local function's return type. Without one, it uses the join, the least common supertype, of its elements' run-time types. Some other cases still get the empty type `Bottom` under walk (`references/revival-changes.md`, "Static parameters").
134	- **Numbers are siblings, not a tower.** `ZZ32`, `ZZ64`, `NN32`, `NN64`, `ZZ`, `QQ`, `RR32` and `RR64` are siblings under `Number`. None is a subtype of another, unlike Haskell's classes or Java's widening. A wider type declares a `coerce` from each narrower one. A conversion never changes which declaration runs when one already fits. Overflow raises `IntegerOverflow`, but an expression of numerals alone folds exactly (`references/revival-changes.md`, "Numbers"). The algebra is self-typed traits, such as `AdditiveGroup[\T\]` with `+`, not monoids over an operator parameter. `references/library.md` gives the rest: ranges, wrapping, `SUM`.
135	- **Loops and reductions are library code.** `for`, comprehensions and `SUM` call the library's generators and reductions (`references/library.md`).
136	- **Juxtaposition is an operator, and whitespace counts.** `f x` applies a function. Otherwise juxtaposition is an operator that the library overloads: `2 x` multiplies, and `"a" "b"` concatenates. How three juxtaposed items group depends on their types, unlike in Haskell. An infix operator has whitespace on both sides or on neither: `a -b` is a static error. Precedence is partial: `a + b ∪ c` needs parentheses.
137	- **Specified, but not built:** dimensions and units, `property` declarations, regions and complex numbers. Some constructs run only under walk (`references/compiler.md`).

141	The record's main files:

143	- `explorations/coordinator/POSITIONS.md`: the curator's decisions.

## Fortress as a language

Each point below corrects an assumption from a language that you know. `references/tests-writing.md` gives the form of a program.

- **Dispatch is on every argument, at run time.** A call chooses among overloads by the run-time types of all its arguments, as in Julia, not by static types as in Java. The checker accepts two overloads only if their parameter types exclude each other, one is strictly more specific, or a third covers their meet. The more specific one's return type must fit the other's. Walk checks part of this at load.
- **Functional methods.** A method with `self` among its parameters is called `f(x)`, not `x.f()`. It overloads with top-level functions. Most operators are declared so: `opr +(self, other: T): T`. A functional method's name is reserved in every program that imports it, so do not name a variable after it. One type must not have a dotted and a functional method of the same name.
- **Traits and objects, no classes.** A trait has methods and abstract fields, and extends several traits. An object is a leaf. `excludes {A, B}` says that no value has both types. `comprises {A, B}` says that every value has a listed type, near Scala's `sealed`. No type may extend two instantiations of one generic trait. This exclusion rule is why the number types are flat (below).
- **Static parameters.** They are written `[\T\]`, and `[i]` indexes. Their kinds are types, sizes (a `nat` or `int` parameter used as a value is a `ZZ32`: `references/revival-changes.md`, "Numbers"), `bool` and `opr`. Generics are invariant: there is no `+T` or `-T`. An unbounded type parameter is bounded by `Any`, which holds tuples, functions and `()`, as `Object` does not. A type parameter that a call does not fix takes its bound. Under walk, one whose bound names the parameter itself stays open, and every value passes it. Walk instantiates a reduction or a comprehension without static arguments at the type declared for its value: a local variable's type, or a top-level or local function's return type. Without one, it uses the join, the least common supertype, of its elements' run-time types. Some other cases still get the empty type `Bottom` under walk (`references/revival-changes.md`, "Static parameters").
- **Numbers are siblings, not a tower.** `ZZ32`, `ZZ64`, `NN32`, `NN64`, `ZZ`, `QQ`, `RR32` and `RR64` are siblings under `Number`. None is a subtype of another, unlike Haskell's classes or Java's widening. A wider type declares a `coerce` from each narrower one. A conversion never changes which declaration runs when one already fits. Overflow raises `IntegerOverflow`, but an expression of numerals alone folds exactly (`references/revival-changes.md`, "Numbers"). The algebra is self-typed traits, such as `AdditiveGroup[\T\]` with `+`, not monoids over an operator parameter. `references/library.md` gives the rest: ranges, wrapping, `SUM`.
- **Loops and reductions are library code.** `for`, comprehensions and `SUM` call the library's generators and reductions (`references/library.md`).
- **Juxtaposition is an operator, and whitespace counts.** `f x` applies a function. Otherwise juxtaposition is an operator that the library overloads: `2 x` multiplies, and `"a" "b"` concatenates. How three juxtaposed items group depends on their types, unlike in Haskell. An infix operator has whitespace on both sides or on neither: `a -b` is a static error. Precedence is partial: `a + b ∪ c` needs parentheses.
- **Specified, but not built:** dimensions and units, `property` declarations, regions and complex numbers. Some constructs run only under walk (`references/compiler.md`).

The record's main files:

- `explorations/coordinator/POSITIONS.md`: the curator's decisions.
- `explorations/coordinator/FACTS.md`: what is established about the original tree. Each fact names its test and points to the report that holds its detail.

The compiler's prelude has no array types, only `ZZ32Vector` and `StringVector`. Its `for` loops, comprehensions and reductions work over `ZZ32` ranges only. Its reductions give a `ZZ32` or a `String`.

Until the switch-over, a compiled test uses none of these. If a test needs one, write it as an `XXX` test that names the wall (`tests-writing.md`).

## What the code generator does

- It emits no primitive `double` arithmetic.
- It runs a program's own `coerce` from a numeral once for each place where the numeral is written, in the component class's static initializer, except at a generic type (below). So a coercion that raises stops the program before `run()`. A test of it sets `run_exits_nonzero=true` (`tests-writing.md`).
- The class loader rewrites a template's bytes with ASM. The emitted classfiles stay at version 1.6, because this rewriting keeps no stack-map frames. Do not raise the version.
- The `value` modifier adds the mark interface `ValueObjectMark` to the object's class. The compiled `SEQV` (`nativeHelpers/equality.java`) reads the mark. The modifier does not inline or unbox the fields.
- An array of `RR64` values is to be stored as an unboxed `double[]`. The code generator does not build it yet. If your task touches how arrays are stored, print the two POSITIONS entries on arrays first (about 2 KB):

      explorations/coordinator/tools/facts-extract.sh 'positions:array is stored as' 'positions:array design'

## The runtime

- The class loader is `runtimeSystem/InstantiatingClassloader.java`. The revival has changed it for sizes and for the lock on a class's first load (ledger row 417). Before you investigate a failure while a class loads, read ledger rows 408 and 559, which name it (`records.md`, "Reading the record").
- The compiled code keeps each mutable variable in a cell (`compiler/runtimeValues/MutableFValue.java`). Before each read and write of the cell, the generated code asks `BaseTask.inATransaction()` (`runtimeSystem/`). Inside an `atomic` block, the access goes through the transaction. So the transaction tracks the variables that the block touches. From the switch-over, it also tracks each element of the one library's arrays, by array and index: `compiler/runtimeValues/FortressArrayStore.java` calls the transaction's methods `TXReadSlot` and `TXWriteSlot`. Walk does not run this class, so test an edit of it with `ArrayStoreJUTest`, beside it.

## Natives

`import java com.sun.fortress.nativeHelpers.{...}` in a `.fss` file binds static Java methods over plain Java values.

A body `builtinPrimitive("com.sun.fortress.nativeHelpers.Class.method")` binds one such method, a helper, too. In a compile, at the parse, the compiled path, and not walk, rewrites the body as a call of the method through a generated `import java`, with `self` first in a trait or object (`compiler/BuiltinPrimitiveRewriter.java`). The checker then checks the declaration against the method's Java signature. In a compile, it reads `int` as `ZZ32`, `long` as `ZZ64`, `float` as `RR32`, `double` as `RR64`, `boolean` as `Boolean`, `String` as `JavaString`, `BigInteger` as `ZZ` and `Object` as `Any` (`NamingCzar.fortressTypeForForeignJavaType`). The compile stops in these cases:

- If the string is in that package but names no public static method: 'builtinPrimitive names no static helper: …'.
- If the string names a glue class or anything else outside that package: 'Variable builtinPrimitive is not defined.'
- If the declaration has a varargs parameter: the same message (ledger row 849).
- If the declaration is a local function or a method of an object expression: the same message. The rewrite reaches only a component's declarations and the members of its traits and objects (ledger row 865).

The rewrite runs only in a JVM that has made a Fortress repository of the compiled path, the compiler's store of components, not this git repository. Walk's repository switches it off again. `fortress compile` makes one, and so do `disambiguate`, `grammar`, `desugar` and `typecheck` (`Shell.compilerPhases`). `fortress parse` and `fortress api` make none, so they rewrite a body only after a compile in the same JVM (ledger row 882). Alone, they pass a misspelt helper. Test a binding with `compile`. In a suite, the result of `parse` or `api` depends on whether a compile ran earlier in the same JVM.

To test a helper on the compiled path, write a compiled test whose own declarations bind it, as `compiler_tests/NativeHelperBindingCompiled.fss` does. Until the switch-over, a compiled test cannot reach the interpreter's library's bindings.

The count stage and the distance stage check the interpreter's library with the same rewrite. There, the checker differs from a compile in these ways:

- A string that names a glue class, or a declaration with a varargs parameter, does not stop the check. The body stays a call of `builtinPrimitive`, typed at the declared result type, and no Java signature checks it (ledger row 849).
- The checker reads a helper's Java types as the interpreter's library's types: `String` as `String`, not `JavaString`, and the rest as in a compile.
- A component that imports a DSL grammar is parsed by other code (`GraphRepository.syntaxExpand`), which does not rewrite its bindings. So, as for a glue class, no Java signature checks them.
- The count stage checks only the `FortressLibrary` component's bindings. A binding of another component, as `FortressBuiltin`'s, only the distance stage checks.

The checker, in a compile and in both stages, reads `int` as `NN32` or `Char`, and `long` as `NN64`, only for six transfer helpers with fixed names (`NamingCzar.java:373-384`, `:494-503`). Where a binding gives a parameter, `self` or the result the type `NN32`, `NN64` or `Char`, or a parameter or `self` the type `UnsignedLong` (the one library's object that extends `NN64`), and the helper has `int` or `long` there, the rewrite passes that value through the matching transfer helper. A result declared `UnsignedLong` gets none. `self` gets a transfer helper only in a method of one of these four types itself. The transfer helpers return their argument unchanged. So the checker accepts such a binding whatever helper it names, a signed one included, as `simpleIntArith.intLT` for `NN32`'s `<`. If you move a binding over these types onto a helper, test it on both paths at values where a signed and an unsigned reading differ (2^31 and above for `NN32`, 2^63 and above for `NN64`), as `compiler_tests/NativeHelperFamilyNN32Compiled.fss` and `tests/NativeHelperFamilyNN32Walk.fss` do. If the class has more than one method of the helper's name and number of parameters, the rewrite adds no transfer helper. The checker then reports 'Could not check call to function builtinPrimitive_<Class>_<method>', followed by '… is not applicable to an argument of type …'.

The wrapper generator wraps every method of a class that it is given, the private methods too. If a type has no Fortress counterpart, it fails the whole import. So give every method of a helper class a signature that maps to Fortress, also a private method. In the count stage and the distance stage, a type maps only if the interpreter's library declares it. So there, a binding stops its component if any method of its helper's class has a type that only the compiler's prelude declares. The distance stage then counts the component as a stopped target. `nativeHelpers/systemOps` is such a class: its `getArgs` answers `StringVector`, so the message is 'FortressBuiltin.StringVector is undefined.' (F-321). Bind a helper of another class.

## Traps of the compiled path

- The compiler's prelude declares `print`, `println` and `String`'s `||` at `Object`, not `Any` (`ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/CompilerBuiltin.fsi:37`, `:55`, `:61`). So until the switch-over, the checker refuses a generic that prints a value of a type parameter written without a bound, or concatenates it onto a `String`. The message names `Object`, as 'Object->() is not applicable to an argument of type T.' does for `println`. In such a generic of a compiled program or test, write `T extends Object`. The generic then takes no tuple, function or `()`. The one library declares these operations at `Any` or `String`, so do not change its text for this limit. The prelude's `||` takes the string first only, so `c || s` for a `Character` value `c` is refused (ledger row 965). Put a string first, as `("" || c) || s`.
- A `try`'s `forbid` clause lists exception types: an exception of a listed type that no `catch` clause took is wrapped in a `ForbiddenException`, which the `try` throws. A `try`'s `finally` clause does not run when an exception leaves the `try` block: one that no `catch` clause takes, or that `ForbiddenException` (ledger row 890). So write no compiled program that relies on `finally` after an exception leaves the `try`. A test that needs it is an `XXX` test (`tests-writing.md`). In a `try` nested in another `try` of one body, the outer `try`'s `catch` clause is matched first (ledger row 888). A `try` whose block can throw, with a `finally` clause and no `catch` or `forbid` clause, fails with a `VerifyError` at class load (ledger row 891).
- Numerals and sizes depart from `revival-changes.md`, "Numbers", in these ways:
  - At a program's own generic type, a numeral's coercion runs at each evaluation (ledger row 957). Bind the value once, at a top-level variable.
  - A negative constant at a program's own number type reaches its coercion with its sign, as -3, not as `-` on the coercion of 3 (ledger row 961).
  - A `nat` or `int` parameter of 2^31 or more, used as a value, raises a `java.lang.Error` that no `catch` sees (ledger row 962). Assert no value for it in a test.
  - As a `typecase`'s selector, a numeral keeps the type `IntLiteral`, so `typecase 7 of ZZ32 => ...` is refused as unreachable (ledger row 963). Bind the selector to a variable first, as `x = 7`, then write `typecase x of ...`.
- A `typecase` tuple pattern with an untyped binder, as `(x, y: ZZ32)`, stops the code generator: 'typcase match failure!' (ledger row 964). Give each binder a type.
- An api and the component that implements it must have the same name. If there is none, the link fails ("Could not find an implementation for API"), and the run dies with `NoClassDefFoundError`.
- The compiled dispatch ignores the contravariance of a parameter of arrow type. The property `fortress.disable.contravariance` is true by default, so `OverloadSet` passes no variance. If a compiled call with function arguments picks another declaration than walk does, look here first.
- A clean link does not prove that every call has its method. Two calls die at run time with `NoSuchMethodError`:
  - a call of a functional method of an object that a trait's `comprises` clause lists, on a value whose static type is the object. An example is `num(R)`, where `trait Q comprises { R }` declares `abstract num(self): ZZ32` and `object R extends Q` gives its body. Call it through a value typed as the trait, as `q: Q = R` and then `num(q)` (ledger row 815);
  - a read of an exported object's value parameter, from a component that imports the api, where the exporting component names the parameter otherwise than the api. A value parameter is a parameter of the object's constructor, and also a field. An example is `Np(3).a`, where the api declares `object Np(a: ZZ32)` and the component `object Np(z: ZZ32)`. The export check compares no value parameter's name. Give each value parameter the api's name (ledger row 839).

== explorations/coordinator/POSITIONS.md, ## Decisions on record, ### The one library and the compiled checker

POSITIONS.md:35
- P-37 **One library, the interpreter's, is the library that the compiler checks.** The interpreter's prelude, `FortressLibrary` and `FortressBuiltin`, becomes the compiled path's prelude in place of the compiler's own, and the compiled path reads the interpreter's library with it. Why: the switch-over spares porting the interpreter's library into the compiler's; the revival develops the checker until it accepts that fuller library. The curator sees the compiler's prelude, its own library files `CompilerLibrary`, `CompilerBuiltin` and `CompilerAlgebra`, as a bootstrap to remove. So no declaration is added to the compiler's prelude, and at the switch-over its three files are deleted and their tests kept (P-38 says which tests are respelled; F-293 holds the compiler's fourth file, `CompilerSystem`). The one exception is the numerals: until the switch-over the prelude carries the design of P-174 and P-176, so that both paths treat a numeral alike before it, and that copy goes with the prelude. The decision settles which files survive, not the designs inside them: the one library takes a design of the prelude's where it is the team's later decision, as it took the prelude's flat shape of the number types. This decision does not stop work on the code generator, which is compiler work under either library.

## The curator's decisions on the library

- Scalar ranges are over `ZZ32` only. A range over another integer type is a static error, and walk stops when it builds one. Write a wider counter as a `ZZ32` loop that widens its index.
- `ZZ32` and numerals convert into `RR64` implicitly. `ZZ64` converts into `RR64` only explicitly, by `asFloat`.
- For arithmetic that wraps on overflow, use the wrapping operators ∔ `DOTPLUS`, ∸ `DOTMINUS` and ⨰ `DOTTIMES`. Parenthesise every such expression fully, because their precedence is stated only among themselves.
- `SUM` and `PROD` are generic over `AdditiveGroup` and `MultiplicativeRing`. Write the element type wherever generators stand in brackets, also where the generators, the body or a declared type fix it: `SUM[\ZZ32\][j <- 0#n] f(j)`. The checker refuses a call without it (ledger row 731). Walk runs such a call at its value's declared type, or else at the join of its elements' run-time types. An empty `SUM` with no static argument written and no declared type gives the integer 0, and an empty `PROD` the integer 1, whatever the body's type (ledger row 716). With a static argument written that is not a number type, such as a user group, an empty or filtered `SUM` ends in `CastError` (ledger row 436).
- An indexed type's index parameter is bounded by `Index` (`revival-changes.md`, "Traits and objects"). `BoundedRange[\I\]` cannot take the bound, because the open range `(:)` stays a range over `Any` (P-56). So its `atMost(n: I): FullRange[\I\]` has the condition `where { I extends Index }`, which each call must meet (`Library/FortressLibrary.fsi`). A type whose static parameter is a range's index type takes the bound too, as `UniformDistribution[\T extends Index\]` over a `FullRange[\T\]` (`Library/Random.fsi`).

lines: - **Dispatch is on every argument, at run time.** A call chooses among overloads by the run-time types of all its arguments, as in Julia, not by static types as in Java. The checker accepts two overloads only if their parameter types exclude each other, one is strictly more specific, or a third covers their meet. The more specific one's return type must fit the other's. Walk checks part of this at load.

- **Functional methods.** A method with `self` among its parameters is called `f(x)`, not `x.f()`. It overloads with top-level functions. Most operators are declared so: `opr +(self, other: T): T`. A functional method's name is reserved in every program that imports it, so do not name a variable after it. One type must not have a dotted and a functional method of the same name.

- **Traits and objects, no classes.** A trait has methods and abstract fields, and extends several traits. An object is a leaf. `excludes {A, B}` says that no value has both types. `comprises {A, B}` says that every value has a listed type, near Scala's `sealed`. No type may extend two instantiations of one generic trait. This exclusion rule is why the number types are flat (below).

-- **Static parameters.** They are written `[\T\]`, and `[i]` indexes. Their kinds are types, sizes (a `nat` or `int` parameter used as a value is a `ZZ32`: `references/revival-changes.md`, "Numbers"), `bool` and `opr`. Generics are invariant: there is no `+T` or `-T`. An unbounded type parameter is bounded by `Any`, which holds tuples, functions and `()`, as `Object` does not. A type parameter that a call does not fix takes its bound. Under walk, one whose bound names the parameter itself stays open, and every value passes it. Walk instantiates a reduction or a comprehension without static arguments at the type declared for its value: a local variable's type, or a top-level or local function's return type. # The library

The library is `Library/` and `ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/`, without the compiler's own files there:

- In `Library/`: the interpreter's prelude, `FortressLibrary.fss` and `.fsi`, and its other components. The compiler's `CompilerLibrary`, `CompilerAlgebra` and `CompilerSystem` are not part of it. `FortressAst.fss` and `.fsi` are generated from `ProjectFortress/astgen/Fortress.ast`: edit that file, never these two.
- In `ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/`: `FortressBuiltin`, `NativeArray` and the rest. The compiler's `CompilerBuiltin` is not part of it.
- `LibraryBuiltin/AnyType`, the top type, belongs to both libraries. After an edit to it, also take the compiled path's step (`build-and-caches.md`, "After an edit of the library").
- `Library/incomplete/` is not on the source path (`default_repository/configuration`), so no program can import what it declares. Nothing that the suites or the model program run imports `Library/GeneratorLibrary.fss` either. Before you cite a declaration as the library's way, check that a running program can reach it.

## How loops and reductions call the library

The desugarer, which both paths share, turns these forms into calls of the library:

- `for x <- g do b end` becomes `g.loop(fn x => b)`, a call of the generator's `loop` method. Each further generator nests one more `loop` call inside.
- `while x <- e do b end` becomes `while __whileCond(e, fn x => b) do end`. `if x <- e then ... end` becomes a call of `__cond`.
- A comprehension or a big operator, such as `SUM`, becomes a call of `__bigOperator`, whose argument calls `__generate` on each generator. So does a big operator inside another: no desugaring calls the library's `__bigOperator2`.

These functions work on the library's generators and reductions: `trait Generator` and `trait Reduction` in `FortressLibrary.fsi`, and `RangeInternals.fss` for ranges. `FortressLibrary.fss` also defines `__loop`, but no desugaring calls it. So a failure inside a loop or a reduction is most often in the library's code, and its fix is a library edit.

## The curator's decisions on the library

- Scalar ranges are over `ZZ32` only. A range over another integer type is a static error, and walk stops when it builds one. Write a wider counter as a `ZZ32` loop that widens its index.
- `ZZ32` and numerals convert into `RR64` implicitly. `ZZ64` converts into `RR64` only explicitly, by `asFloat`.
- For arithmetic that wraps on overflow, use the wrapping operators ∔ `DOTPLUS`, ∸ `DOTMINUS` and ⨰ `DOTTIMES`. Parenthesise every such expression fully, because their precedence is stated only among themselves.
- `SUM` and `PROD` are generic over `AdditiveGroup` and `MultiplicativeRing`. Write the element type wherever generators stand in brackets, also where the generators, the body or a declared type fix it: `SUM[\ZZ32\][j <- 0#n] f(j)`. The checker refuses a call without it (ledger row 731). Walk runs such a call at its value's declared type, or else at the join of its elements' run-time types. An empty `SUM` with no static argument written and no declared type gives the integer 0, and an empty `PROD` the integer 1, whatever the body's type (ledger row 716). With a static argument written that is not a number type, such as a user group, an empty or filtered `SUM` ends in `CastError` (ledger row 436).
- An indexed type's index parameter is bounded by `Index` (`revival-changes.md`, "Traits and objects"). `BoundedRange[\I\]` cannot take the bound, because the open range `(:)` stays a range over `Any` (P-56). So its `atMost(n: I): FullRange[\I\]` has the condition `where { I extends Index }`, which each call must meet (`Library/FortressLibrary.fsi`). A type whose static parameter is a range's index type takes the bound too, as `UniformDistribution[\T extends Index\]` over a `FullRange[\T\]` (`Library/Random.fsi`).
- An array's `fill` takes a value, and its `tabulate` a function of the index: `array[\ZZ32\](4).fill(0)`, `array[\ZZ32\](4).tabulate(fn (i:ZZ32):ZZ32 => 10 i)`. The factories that take a function are `tabulatedArray1` to `tabulatedArray3` and `tabulatedVector`.

## Designing a change

- Put each extension into this library, outside the compiler's files. This includes an extension that only the model program needs.
- Fix a gap in the library, not by a workaround in the program that meets it. Take the design from the library's practice as well as from the specification's text. If the two disagree, do as `specification.md`, "When the text and an implementation disagree", says.
- If a rule of the language or the checker refuses the way that you want, find how the library writes that kind of thing. Do the same. The checker's refusals of this library reach you through your brief, or through a run of the count stage (`compiler.md`): `fortress typecheck` checks against the compiler's prelude.
- When you add a method, make it dotted or functional as its family in the library does. If the family shows no practice, follow the team's proposal, which no program can import (`Library/incomplete/Collection.fss`): an updater, a getter or a setter, indexing included, is dotted, and every other method is functional.
- A new functional method reserves its name in every program that imports the library. The phase that binds names then refuses each program that names a variable or a parameter after it: "Variable even is already declared."
- A `fail` without a static argument has the result type `Any`. Where it must have a type, write the static argument, as `strToInt` calls `fail[\ZZ32\]`.
- A dotted method shadows a top-level function of the same name (`overloading.tex`, "Principles of Overloading").
- In an api, declare each top-level function and each member of a trait or object at the header that the component gives it. A function's header is its name, its static parameters with their bounds, its modifiers, its `throws` clause, its parameters' modifiers and types, and its return type. A function's parameters' names and a `where` clause do not count, but each static parameter's name counts (ledger row 836). Give an object's value parameters the api's names, because they are its fields (`compiler.md`, "Traps of the compiled path"). In the cases below, change the component's header to the api's, not the api's to the component's. The examples are in `Library/FortressLibrary.fsi` and `Library/FortressLibrary.fss`.
  - The member's body already answers the api's type. `RR64`'s `opr |\self/|`, `opr |/self\|` and `truncate` answer `ZZ64`, because they call `Float`'s natives, which answer `ZZ64` (`ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/FortressBuiltin.fss:184-191`).
  - The api cannot name the component's type. `Array2`'s and `Array3`'s `bounds` and `zeroIndices` answered types of `RangeInternals`, which depends on this api. They now answer the api's `CompactFullRange` types, which those types extend.
  - The api's type is wider, and the overrides and bodies use only that type. `DelegatedIndexed`'s `generator` answers the api's `Generator[\E\]`, as `FlatString`'s override does.

  In the api, write `abstract` on each member that the component leaves without a body.
- The compiled checker's export check matches each api member with a component member of the same name and header. It matches these members in these ways:
  - A field, as `x: ZZ32` in an api's trait: by a component field of its name, its type and its modifiers other than `var`. A component's getter does not match it, so declare a field in the component too (ledger row 842).
  - An object's value parameter: by its type and its modifiers other than `var`, but not by its name.
  - A getter written `abstract`, as `abstract getter one(): T`: by a component getter at its header, or by a component field of its name and type that is neither `hidden` nor `private`. A `hidden` field has no getter.
  - Another member written `abstract`: by a component member at the api's header, with a body or without one.

  Each entry of the check's error names a trait or object and only its first member that differs. After you fix that member, check again to see the next. These steps run the check:
  - For a component of a compiled program or test: `fortress compile`.
  - For the one library's `FortressLibrary` component: the count stage (`compiler.md`, "The checker's time").
  - For the other thirteen components that the gate's distance stage checks: that stage. When a rung needs it, the brief gives its command.
  - For another component of the one library: no step, until the switch-over.
- A new overload can make walk refuse every program at load. `interpreter.md`, "What walk checks", lists what walk refuses.
- Write a new native as a public static method of a class under `nativeHelpers/`, and bind it with `builtinPrimitive("com.sun.fortress.nativeHelpers.Class.method")`. Both paths run it. Give it the Java types that carry the declared types (`interpreter.md`, "Natives"). Write a glue class under `interpreter/glue/prim/`, which only walk runs, only where no Java type carries a declared type, as for the bindings in `Library/Reflect.fss`. A native is an edit of Java: rebuild (`build-and-caches.md`, "Two layers of code"), and test it on both paths (`compiler.md`, "Natives").
- `interpreter.md`, "The model program", says how to check microGPT under walk.

## Editing

A comment after a declaration that ends in an expression or a type becomes part of that declaration's source span. It also becomes part of the unambiguous name made from the span. So a comment-only edit changes the syntax tree. Before you compare parse trees or diagnostics across such an edit, map their positions back to the lines before the edit. Three removed scripts did this: `parse-compare.sh`, `ast-compare.py` and `remap-lines.py`. Print one with `git show ab067d9b6^:explorations/compile-ladder/rung-library-comments/<name>`.

I've brought the `fortress-repo` skill in line with climb batch 29b's landing, in two commits. Lint is clean on every changed file, and nothing is pushed.

## Commits
- `27cb304a2a`: "fortress-repo: climb batch 29b landing, the orientation update installed". It changes `references/revival-changes.md` and `references/sources.md`.
- `1bcb6fac1c`: "fortress-repo: climb batch 29b landing, the area parts brought in line". It changes `SKILL.md`, `compiler.md`, `interpreter.md`, `library.md` and `sources.md`.

## Sections installed from the orientation
The judge marked two sections "install" and held none. Neither commit touched the other five parts, which are identical in both files.

- **"Static parameters, `where` clauses and sizes"**: the paragraph on `reflect` is shorter, and every rule in it stays.
- **"Numbers"**: the old text gave numeral forms that now fail, such as the getters, `coerce(x: IntLiteral)` and `asFloat` on a numeral type. It also said that `(h = 0.5)` is `true`, which is now `false` under walk.
  - It now gives the numeral types with their four numbers as static arguments, and the coercion that is generic over those numbers, with its `where` clause.
  - It now says that `RR64` and `RR32` on the compiled path take only `3.0`, not `3`.
  - It now gives the binding form for comparing a typed value with a numeral, and the fold's rule for a program's own type.
  - I applied the judge's two corrections. First, the checker *does* refuse a numeral that breaks the `where` clause, with 'The numeral 300 does not meet the where clause of the coercion to Byte.' I checked this against `CoercionOracle.scala:221` and the test. Second, a negated numeral is excepted from the fold sentence.
- **Size**: the file goes from 28,031 to 29,291 bytes, as the judge predicted. The judge accepted the size exception, and reports the budget conflict to the coordinator.

## Sentences changed (commit `1bcb6fac1c`)
- **`SKILL.md`, "Static parameters"**: it said that any `nat` or `int` parameter used as a value is a `ZZ32`. It now says "a `nat` or `int` parameter that is a size, used as a value, is a `ZZ32`". The reason is that a coercion reads a numeral's four numbers as `ZZ` (P-173, P-174, F-342).
- **`interpreter.md`, walk's departures**:
  - Row 960 named the deleted `digits` getter. It now says "so a coercion reads the digit count of `00.5` as 2, not 3".
  - Row 966's workaround was `NOT (u = 0)`. That gives a silent wrong `true`, because `u = 0` is now `false` (row 973). It now says "Bind the numeral at the type first, as `z: NN32 = 0`, then write `u =/= z`." This is the row's own workaround.
  - The bullet on row 968 is deleted, because the row is fixed (`a26e74f5c`).
  - A new bullet for row 974: a numeral type written as a static argument, or as a type that an object or a trait extends, loads and runs under walk. The compiled checker refuses both forms.
- **`compiler.md`, "The compiler's prelude"**: it now adds "The one exception is the numerals: until the switch-over, the prelude carries their design (P-37)."
- **`compiler.md`, "What the code generator does"**: it said "except at a generic type". It now says "except where the place's type names a type parameter". This follows row 957 and `CodeGen.java`, `numeralCoercionSiteDesc`.
- **`compiler.md`, "Traps of the compiled path"**:
  - Row 957 is restated: "At a place whose type names a type parameter of its generic declaration … Bind the value once, at a top-level variable of an instance type."
  - The bullet on row 961 is deleted, because the row is fixed.
  - Row 963 said that the selector keeps the type `IntLiteral`. It now says it keeps "its own type, as `NaturalNumeral[\1,10,7\]`".
  - New trap for row 971: a numeral coercion that spawns a task fails the class's load. Bind the two calls to locals first.
  - New trap for row 442's numeral half: `r: RR64 = 3` is refused. Write `3.0`. I checked this against `CompilerBuiltin.fsi:401-403` and `:444`.
- **`library.md`, line 23**: it now adds that until the switch-over, the compiled path converts into `RR64` only a numeral with a radix point and an `RR32` (row 442).

## Already true, or nothing to change
- **The changed decisions (POSITIONS)**: no sentence of the skill rests on any of their old words. I searched with `git grep` and changed nothing.
- **Row 962 in `compiler.md`**: still true.
- **The three points marked "not taken"** (F-58's `^`, F-79's prelude clause, F-169's "four numbers"): I left them as they are.

## Choices and decisions not taken
- **The two corrections**: the task said to copy "word for word", and the judge's install said to apply the two corrections. I followed the judge. The other way was to install the text as written, which keeps a false sentence.
- **Row 442 is now stated twice**: once in `revival-changes.md` and once as a trap in `compiler.md`. The data asked for the trap. The other way is to keep it only in "Numbers".
- **No separate bullet for row 973 in `interpreter.md`**: "Numbers" already states walk's answer, with the row. Adding a bullet would duplicate it.

## For the coordinator
- **`SKILL.md:71`**: it still says that the fold gives "a numeral, a quotient of two numerals or a boolean". The orientation now says "one exact constant". No list named this line, so I left it.
- **`compiler.md` is over its 30,000-character mark**: it went from 31,219 to 31,700 bytes. It was already over before this landing.
- **Uncommitted files**: `regression/key.md`, `regression/questions.md` and the orientation folder are not committed. They are not mine. The judge also notes that three lines of the key are stale against the installed text.
- **Not yet checked**: no cold read or quiz has run on the two corrections. The cold read of the installed part is due.
- **Other skills**: no other skill holds a sentence that this landing made false.
- **Shell**: the shell would not run commands that hold a variable, or a Python script from the scratchpad, without approval. So I made every edit with the Edit tool.
